newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Jan 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Jan 23.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Thursday's Wall Street Journal:
* PepsiCo Inc is expected to spin off its $11 billion restaurant business. The company's board is meeting today and could make an announcement.
The company is also seeking to change its contract with bottlers to gain an edge over Coca-Cola.
* ConAgra has agreed to pay millions in penalties to settle an investigation into the unit's practice of spraying water on stored grain.
* Oil companies could pay $100 million more a year because of new government regulations.
* A Philip Morris lobbyist testified that the company asked two business groups to help pay for Mississippi Gov. Kirk Fordice's effort to block the state's suit against the tobacco industry.
* Volkswagen AG confirmed it has an agreement to build cars in Russia, and General Motors said it is discussing the possibility of similar deals.
* AT&T reported a 12 percent higher fourth quarter profit excluding year-ago charges.
* The Securities and Exchange Commission narrowed its investigation into abuses in the municipal bond market to about two dozen bond deals from as many as 100.
* A federal jury ordered Walt Disney Co's ABC to pay Food Lion $5.5 million in damages.
* Federal Express is dropping its flat rate pricing.
* A Federal Reserve survey of its district banks shows the economy growing at a moderate pace.
* Housing starts fell 12.2 percent in December.
* The dollar rose to a four-year high against the yen and a 31-month high against the mark.
* The Dow Jones industrials fell 33.87 to 6850.03.

* As the nation's real estate investment trusts announce their year-end numbers, many will be reporting record results. Such gains have already helped REIT stocks outpace the overall market, with total returns last year of 36 percent, counting price change plus dividends.

The trouble is, industry analysts say, many of those reports will be inflated by a variety of controversial, yet perfectly legal, accounting tactics, which allow REITs to pump up their numbers with revenue they haven't yet received, or to treat certain expenses as if they never occurred. -- Heard on the Street.

* Bond prices resumed a recent downward trend on Wednesday as investors, lacking a conviction on the outlook for interest rates, sold Treasury securities to buy higher-yielding corporate bonds and prepare for the release of important economic statistics. -- Credit Markets.
